raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old male patient with no prior medical history presented to the emergency room with high-grade fever for 2 days. He also had chills, headaches, muscle aches, fatigue, and diarrhea. He used over-the-counter acetaminophen to control his symptoms.
On admission, the patient was oriented. His temperature was 38 C, blood pressure was 130/90 mmHg, pulse was 92 bpm, respirations were 20 bpm, and oxygen saturation was 98%. Physical examination showed no abdominal pain, no organomegaly, a negative Murphy's sign, and no evidence of mucocutaneous bleeding. Laboratory tests were significant for thrombocytopenia with platelet count of 67.000/mm3, high hematocrit (45%), hemoglobin level of 15.2 g/dL, leukocyte count of 3.310/mm3, and a positive NS1 antigen test. His liver enzymes were mildly elevated, AST was 89 U/L, and ALT was 69 U/L; serum HbsAg and HCV antibody were negative. Serum creatinine and C-reactive protein were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver and pancreas sizes, thickening gallbladder wall (8 mm), and no intraperitoneal fluid was noted. Chest X-ray was unremarkable.
In the hospital, his diarrhea was worsening, more than 5 times a day. On the fifth day after the onset of fever, he started to have burning-like abdominal pain, which was localized in the epigastrium and radiated to the back. He had 2-3 episodes of nausea and vomiting per day. He also developed petechiae over his lower limbs. Laboratory results showed elevated serum amylase (174 U/L) and lipase (606 U/L). Platelet count decreased to 10.000/U, hematocrit was 51%, leukocyte count was 5.200/mm3, and serum triglyceride was 3.81 mmol/L (Table 1). Plain abdominal computed tomography revealed an enlarged pancreas, peripancreatic fat stranding, and peripancreatic fluid collection (Balthazar score D) along with a minimal right pleural effusion (Figure 1). He was managed with intravenous fluids, analgesics, antacid, and bowel rest. Two days later, his clinical condition became stable, he started to be afebrile, the abdominal pain was resolved, and his platelet cell count was trending up. Subsequently, he was discharged without complications.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presented with high-grade fever for 2 days associated with chills, headaches, muscle aches, fatigue, and diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-day history of acute high-grade fever, chills, headaches, myalgias, fatigue, and diarrhea, for which he had taken over-the-counter acetaminophen. Following admission, diarrhea worsened to more than five episodes daily. On illness day 5, he developed severe, burning-like epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back, accompanied by 2-3 daily episodes of nausea and vomiting, as well as a new petechial rash over his lower extremities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever, chills, headaches, fatigue, generalized muscle aches, diarrhea, epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Home medications included over-the-counter acetaminophen.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 38 C, blood pressure 130/90 mmHg, pulse 92 bpm, respiratory rate 20 bpm, SpO2 98%. Patient was oriented. Abdominal examination revealed no tenderness, no organomegaly, and a negative Murphy's sign on admission. No mucocutaneous bleeding on admission; by illness day 5, petechiae developed over the bilateral lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations:
Admission investigations: Platelet count 67,000/mm3, hematocrit 45%, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL, leukocyte count 3,310/mm3, AST 89 U/L, ALT 69 U/L. Serum creatinine and C-reactive protein were within normal limits. Viral hepatitis serologies (HBsAg and anti-HCV) were negative.
Abdominal ultrasound: Normal liver and pancreas sizes, gallbladder wall thickening (8 mm), and absence of intraperitoneal fluid.
Chest X-ray: Unremarkable.
Hospital day 5 investigations: Platelet count dropped to 10,000/uL, hematocrit rose to 51%, leukocyte count 5,200/mm3, serum amylase 174 U/L, serum lipase 606 U/L, serum triglycerides 3.81 mmol/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Plain abdominal computed tomography (CT): Enlarged pancreas with peripancreatic fat stranding and peripancreatic fluid collection (Balthazar score D), along with a minimal right pleural effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue fever complicated by acute pancreatitis, severe thrombocytopenia, and plasma leakage, confirmed by a positive NS1 antigen test. Acute hepatitis B (HBsAg negative) and hepatitis C (anti-HCV negative) were ruled out.
Treatment and outcome: Managed with intravenous fluid resuscitation, analgesics, antacids, and strict bowel rest. Two days later, clinical status stabilized, patient became afebrile, abdominal pain resolved, and platelet counts trended upward. Discharged without further complications.
